title: Types of Teeth
keyIdea: Human teeth come in four types, and each shape fits a job. Incisors at the front are flat and sharp like chisels: they cut and bite. Canines next to them are long and pointed: they grip and tear. Premolars, with two bumps, crush food, and the wide, bumpy molars at the back grind it into tiny bits. Each quarter of an adult mouth has 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars and 3 molars, so an adult has 32 teeth. Children have 20 milk teeth, with no premolars. Animal teeth match their food: meat eaters have long canines and slicing back teeth, plant eaters have wide, flat grinding teeth.
familyTip: At dinner, take a bite of something crunchy like an apple or carrot. Notice which teeth bite the piece off and which teeth chew it up. Then look in a mirror together and count the teeth in one quarter of your mouth.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: find 4 tooth types in a jaw, match foods to tooth jobs, build adult and milk-tooth quarters, and sort animals by their teeth.

kid: Your teeth are not all the same. Scientists sort them into four types by their shape. Each shape is good at one job. Eating starts in your mouth, where teeth break food into small bits that are easy to swallow.

Incisors are the flat, sharp teeth at the front. They cut and bite, like scissors. Canines sit next to them. They are long and pointed, for gripping and tearing. Further back are premolars, with two bumps, for crushing. At the very back are molars. They are the widest teeth, with bumpy tops, for grinding food into mush.

Your mouth has four quarters. In an adult, each quarter has 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars and 3 molars. That is 8 teeth, and 4 quarters make 32. Children have a first set of 20 milk teeth with no premolars. Milk teeth fall out from about age 6, and adult teeth grow in.

Animal teeth fit their food too. A lion has long canines and sharp back teeth that slice meat. A horse has wide, flat back teeth to grind grass. People eat both plants and meat, so we have a mix of tooth types.
adult: Ages 8 to 9. The National Curriculum in England asks Year 4 pupils to identify the different types of teeth in humans and their simple functions, as part of the animals including humans unit on digestion. It also links to NGSS 4-LS1-1 (internal and external structures support survival). Tooth counts and jobs follow the NHS and the Oral Health Foundation: adults have 8 incisors, 4 canines, 8 premolars and 12 molars (32, counting wisdom teeth), and children have 20 milk teeth with no premolars.

The lab has five tasks. Learners tap a jaw to find the four tooth shapes, then drag four eating jobs to the teeth that do them. They build one adult quarter from front to back and see four quarters make 32. They sort six animals by diet from their teeth, then build a milk-tooth quarter alone and see why it makes 20.

Common mistakes. Children often call every back tooth a molar and miss premolars, or think canines are for chewing. Many think teeth are all one shape in different sizes. When counting they may double the 16 in one jaw wrongly or mix up the milk set of 20 and the adult set of 32. With animals, take care: having no canines does not mean an animal cannot eat well, as rabbits and horses show.

practice.prompt: Which teeth bite a piece off an apple?
practice.hint: Which teeth are flat and sharp at the front?
practice.explain: Incisors are flat and sharp, like chisels. They cut and bite. Molars and premolars are at the back and crush and grind.

practice.prompt: Each quarter of an adult mouth has 8 teeth. How many teeth are in {n} quarters?
practice.hint: Multiply the teeth in one quarter by the number of quarters.
practice.explain: 8 teeth × {n} quarters = {=8*n} teeth. All 4 quarters make 32.
Long, pointed canines grip and tear. Incisors cut, and molars grind.

practice.prompt: A child has 20 milk teeth. {n} have fallen out so far. How many milk teeth are left?
practice.hint: Take the fallen-out teeth away from 20.
practice.explain: 20 − {n} = {=20-n} milk teeth left. Adult teeth grow in where the milk teeth fell out.

practice.prompt: A horse has wide, flat back teeth and no big canines. What does it eat?
practice.hint: What are wide, flat teeth good at?
practice.explain: Wide, flat teeth grind tough plants like grass. Meat eaters need long canines and slicing back teeth.

pool.prompt: Which teeth grind food into tiny bits?
pool.hint: Think of the widest teeth at the back.
pool.explain: Molars are wide with bumpy tops, so they grind. Incisors cut and canines tear.

pool.prompt: Going from the front to the back of one quarter, what is the order?
pool.hint: The cutting teeth are in the middle front, the grinders at the back.
pool.explain: Front to back: 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars, 3 molars. Shapes change from cutting to grinding.

pool.prompt: An adult has 3 molars in each quarter of the mouth. How many molars in {n} quarters?
pool.explain: 3 molars × {n} quarters = {=3*n} molars. A full adult mouth has 12.

pool.prompt: A skull has long, pointed canines and sharp back teeth for slicing. What did the animal eat?
pool.hint: What are pointed teeth good for?
pool.explain: Long canines grip prey and sharp back teeth slice meat. Plant eaters have flat grinding teeth instead.

pool.prompt: Which teeth do children's milk teeth NOT include?
pool.explain: A milk quarter has 2 incisors, 1 canine and 2 molars. Premolars only come with the adult teeth.

pool.prompt: Ben counts {n} teeth in his top jaw. He has the same number in his bottom jaw. How many teeth is that?
pool.hint: The bottom jaw has the same number as the top jaw, so add the two together.
pool.explain: {n} + {n} = {=2*n} teeth. Top and bottom jaws match.

pool.prompt: Why do people have incisors, canines and molars?
choices: People eat both plants and meat
pool.hint: A mix of teeth suits a mix of food.
pool.explain: Humans are omnivores, so we have teeth for cutting, tearing and grinding many kinds of food.

pool.prompt: Mia says canines are for chewing food into mush. What is right?
choices: Canines grip and tear; molars grind food into mush
pool.hint: Which teeth are pointed and which are wide?
pool.explain: Pointed canines grip and tear. The wide, bumpy molars at the back grind food into mush.

pool.hint: They have two bumps and sit just behind the canines.
pool.explain: Premolars crush food before the molars grind it. Incisors cut and canines grip.
